routes.description: Establish a sufficiently reliable historical core of Jesus' death, the empty tomb, and postmortem appearances, then show that a bodily resurrection explains that combined evidence within a relevant theistic background framework.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the historical premises are adequately supported, the appearances are properly interpreted as bodily encounters, competing explanations lack comparable cumulative scope, and resurrection is rationally admissible given the relevant background evidence.

motionBridge.description: Connect the supported historical facts and comparative explanation to the conclusion that Jesus' bodily resurrection is rational.

centralBridges.description: Establish an early and sufficiently reliable source basis for the death, empty tomb, and reported appearances.
Show that the reported experiences and relevant texts concern bodily encounters rather than solely disembodied or private experiences.
Show that resurrection accounts for the combined evidence without requiring the unsupported conjunctions attributed to rival explanations.
Supply relevant background grounds under which resurrection is not excluded solely by ordinary expectations about death.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Support actual death and an empty burial place as constraints on survival, vision-only, and body-removal accounts.
Use cumulative theistic or postmortem-awareness considerations only insofar as they bear on the antecedent plausibility of resurrection.

routes.description: Show that the partisan and incomplete historical record underdetermines what occurred, that nonphysical experiences or unknown body-removal scenarios remain available, and that a miracle conclusion requires background commitments not established by the reports alone.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the evidence cannot securely establish a publicly observable risen body, ordinary or unresolved alternatives remain live, or the prior theological requirements for identifying the event as divine resurrection are not independently warranted.

motionBridge.description: Connect evidential underdetermination and the demanding miracle standard to withholding a bodily-resurrection conclusion.

centralBridges.description: Establish that source dates, partisanship, eyewitness status, and limited independent corroboration restrict the warranted historical inference.
Preserve a reasonable interpretation of the reported experiences that does not establish tangible, publicly observable bodily encounters.
Show that psychological experiences, unknown removal scenarios, or other unresolved possibilities prevent a unique resurrection inference.
Require justified beliefs about a supernatural agent and its intentions before identifying an extraordinary report as a resurrection miracle.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Test whether touching narratives and Pauline spiritual-body language actually establish bodily continuity and physical interaction.
Apply an evidential threshold appropriate to extraordinary perception and postmortem-awareness reports used to alter prior probability.

sections.title: Historical Sources and Early Testimony
sections.rationale: The reliability, dating, independence, and eyewitness connections of the surviving testimony determine what historical premises may enter either side's inference.

sections.title: Death, Burial, and the Empty Tomb
sections.rationale: Actual death and the condition of the burial place constrain survival, vision-only, body-removal, and resurrection accounts without alone deciding among them.

sections.title: Bodily Character of the Reported Appearances
sections.rationale: The motion specifically concerns bodily resurrection, making physical contact, group observation, Pauline terminology, and public corroboration a distinct burden-bearing issue.

sections.title: Naturalistic Alternatives and Explanatory Scope
sections.rationale: The comparative inference depends on whether grief visions, conversion phenomena, collective experiences, removal scenarios, or combinations of them explain the historical claims.

sections.title: Prior Probability and the Miracle Framework
sections.rationale: The rationality of accepting an extraordinary conclusion depends partly on how natural-law expectations, theistic background beliefs, and alleged postmortem evidence bear on prior plausibility.

moves.speaker: Gary Habermas
moves.proposition: Habermas identifies a broadly accepted historical core that includes Jesus' crucifixion, reported appearances, transformed disciples, and the conversions of James and Paul.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly hands the discussion to Habermas, and the uninterrupted answer presents his historical-facts case.

response.rationale: This constructive move supplies the principal asserted historical facts on which the later explanatory case depends.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it clearly presents a relevant factual foundation but compresses the support for acceptance of the listed facts.

precisionFindings.rationale: The historical core is recoverable, but the degree and constituency of scholarly acceptance are only loosely delimited.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Habermas distinguishes the less widely accepted empty tomb, though the broader consensus language exceeds the evidence shown in this span.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The listed facts form a coherent historical foundation, with the later inferential connection to resurrection still unstated here.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The span identifies asserted consensus and several facts but does not provide representative documentation or defend their evidential independence.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly addresses the central historical-foundation bridge and ranks near the top of that tier, though it does not itself complete the motion inference.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move states a constructive inventory and does not meaningfully interpret a developed opposing alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt identifies reported appearances, transformed disciples, Jerusalem preaching, and the cases of James and Paul while qualifying acceptance of the empty tomb.

moves.speaker: Antony Flew
moves.proposition: Uncertain dating, Christian partisanship, the Gospel writers' lack of eyewitness status, and the absence of independent Jerusalem testimony seriously limit the historical warrant supplied by the surviving sources.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator addresses Flew, whose first-person answer directly identifies the deficiencies he sees in the historical record.

components.text: Whether the asserted historical core rests on sources sufficient to warrant treating its components as established.
Whether broad acceptance can substitute for source independence and eyewitness connection.

response.rationale: Flew directly challenges the source basis underlying the asserted historical core by identifying partisanship, non-eyewitness authorship, and missing independent Jerusalem testimony.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The reply expressly contacts the decisive evidential premise supporting the earlier historical inventory, although its dating point is less fully developed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The source criticism is clear, but phrases such as all evidence and absolutely nothing require an implicit restriction to the relevant surviving evidence.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The identified source limitations warrant caution, but categorical statements about all evidence and total absence of testimony are broader than demonstrated.

charity.alternative: Partisan sources can still preserve reliable history, and early Christian testimony may connect with eyewitnesses.
charity.decisiveQualification: Partisanship alone does not defeat testimony, but independence, dating, and eyewitness connection still require specific defense.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from limited independence and eyewitness access to reduced historical confidence is valid, with no claim that partisanship alone proves falsity.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Specific source features are identified, but the universal and absolute formulations are not documented or carefully bounded in the excerpt.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move squarely supports the central source-limitations bridge by attacking the reliability conditions of the historical foundation.

representationalCharity.rationale: Flew relies on several concrete source limitations rather than dismissing testimony merely because it is Christian, though he compresses their individual force.

moves.evidenceBasis: Flew expressly cites uncertain biographical dating, believing Christian authorship, lack of Gospel-writer eyewitness status, and absent testimony from Jerusalem's wider population.

moves.speaker: Gary Habermas
moves.proposition: The early tradition in First Corinthians 15 connects Paul with Peter and James and provides exceptionally early testimony from named eyewitnesses to reported appearances.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator requests an example, and Habermas gives a sustained first-person exposition of First Corinthians 15 and Galatians.

components.text: Whether the record lacks sufficiently early testimony connected to identifiable eyewitnesses.
Whether Christian partisanship and Gospel authorship exhaust the available historical source basis.
Whether independent non-Christian or Jerusalem corroboration is available.

response.rationale: The Pauline tradition directly answers the claimed eyewitness and dating deficiencies but does not supply the requested independent non-Christian or wider Jerusalem corroboration.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This is a strong partial answer contacting the decisive early-eyewitness component while leaving the independent-corroboration component unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The Pauline-source claim is readily recoverable, though transmission from Peter and James is presented with an implicit inferential qualification.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The passage appropriately says the tradition seems to derive from Peter and James, but exceptionally early eyewitness testimony slightly compresses the transmission warrant.

charity.alternative: Early Christian tradition may remain partisan and does not provide independent non-Christian corroboration.
charity.decisiveQualification: Early partisan testimony can answer dating and eyewitness-access concerns without answering the separate independence concern.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from Paul's contact with Peter and James to early access to appearance tradition is coherent, subject to an implicit transmission premise.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Named texts, persons, and a proposed transmission route provide specific support, with one bounded gap concerning derivation of the list from those meetings.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly attacks the central source-limitations bridge through early named testimony, though it leaves independent corroboration unresolved.

representationalCharity.rationale: Habermas fairly supplies evidence responsive to two source objections without claiming that Paul supplies non-Christian corroboration.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt connects First Corinthians 15 with Peter and James, names them alongside Paul, and characterizes the appearance list as exceptionally early historical material.

moves.speaker: Antony Flew
moves.proposition: The disciples' reported experiences can be interpreted as grief-related visions, while Paul's experience can be interpreted as a dramatic psychological religious conversion rather than observation of a risen body.
moves.attributionBasis: Flew is directly invited to explain the agreed experiences and gives both the grief-vision proposal and his psychological account of Paul.

components.text: Whether reported appearance experiences require observation of a risen physical body.
Whether Paul's early appearance testimony establishes a bodily encounter rather than a conversion experience.
Whether the disciples' transformation requires resurrection as its cause.

response.rationale: Flew contacts the interpretation of the disciples' and Paul's experiences by proposing grief visions and conversion psychology, but does not explain all listed historical consequences.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The reply contacts the decisive appearance-interpretation component but leaves group scope, empty-tomb implications, and transformation substantially untreated.

precisionFindings.rationale: The two-part alternative is clear, but Flew rejects the moderator's conversion-psychosis label and leaves the exact psychological mechanism broad.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Flew offers interpretive possibilities and explicitly hesitates over the stronger psychosis terminology, matching the limited support presented.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Grief visions and conversion experiences are logically compatible with the reports, but compatibility alone leaves a material explanatory-scope bridge unstated.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The appeal to familiar conversion phenomena and William James is suggestive but supplies no representative evidence addressing these witnesses or group claims.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly supports the central nonbodily-interpretation bridge, although its explanatory reach is incomplete.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move proposes alternatives to the earlier account but does not materially characterize or evaluate a developed competing explanation.

moves.evidenceBasis: Flew distinguishes grief-related experiences for disciples from a spectacular religious-conversion model for Paul and expressly avoids the stronger psychosis characterization.

moves.speaker: Gary Habermas
moves.proposition: Grief hallucinations do not jointly explain the reported group appearances, varied witnesses and settings, empty tomb, and lasting transformation of the disciples.
moves.attributionBasis: Habermas announces his transition to grief hallucinations and continues the same answer until the moderator solicits Flew's response.

components.text: Whether grief visions and conversion experiences explain the reported range and consequences of the appearances.
Whether the underlying reports are sufficiently reliable and independent to establish that range.
Whether hallucinations account for lasting transformation and the empty tomb.

response.rationale: Habermas directly tests the scope of the psychological account against varied witnesses, settings, transformation, and the empty tomb, while assuming the reliability of those reports.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The reply strongly contacts the alternative's explanatory scope but does not answer the separate source-reliability challenge on which the reported diversity depends.

precisionFindings.rationale: The cumulative objection is clear and the transformation claim is qualified as a general rule, though the exact group reports remain unspecified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The general-rule qualification is appropriate, but the broad dismissal of hallucination accounts outruns the anecdotal research reference in the excerpt.

charity.alternative: Different witnesses could have distinct grief or conversion experiences without sharing one hallucination.
charity.decisiveQualification: A differentiated psychological account remains possible but must explain the reported group, situational, tomb, and transformation evidence jointly.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The cumulative-scope inference is coherent: a rival explaining only individual experiences does not yet explain the full asserted evidence set.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move names several evidence classes but relies on an unnamed friend's research and does not verify the reports or transformation generalization.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central alternative-underdetermination bridge by challenging whether the proposed psychological alternatives cover the combined evidence.

representationalCharity.rationale: Habermas recognizes multiple people and settings and presses cumulative scope rather than treating the alternative as necessarily one shared hallucination.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt contrasts hallucination accounts with varied people and settings, an asserted empty tomb, and the claimed absence of transformative effects as a general rule.

moves.speaker: Antony Flew
moves.proposition: The severe shortage of non-Christian evidence leaves a broad background of historical ignorance, so the record cannot confidently establish what happened or warrant a publicly observable physical-resurrection account.
moves.attributionBasis: Flew answers the moderator's question in the first person and states the epistemic limits he believes the evidence imposes.

components.text: Whether early Christian appearance testimony supplies enough evidence for confident conclusions about what physically occurred.
Whether the accepted fact list can support a confident reconstruction despite extensive missing evidence.
Whether the reported diversity and transformation defeat nonphysical alternatives.

response.rationale: Flew directly argues that sparse non-Christian evidence limits confidence in any reconstruction, but does not engage the particular cumulative objections to hallucination explanations.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive sufficiency question at a general epistemic level while leaving the detailed Pauline and explanatory-scope warrants largely unexamined.

precisionFindings.rationale: The confidence-limiting claim is clear and expressly qualified, though the boundary of the asserted historical ignorance is not specified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move argues against great confidence rather than asserting a contrary reconstruction, appropriately matching its underdetermination evidence.

charity.alternative: The available Christian evidence may still support limited historical conclusions despite missing non-Christian sources.
charity.decisiveQualification: Sparse corroboration does not erase all evidence, but it can restrict confidence in the specifically physical reconstruction.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from extensive evidential gaps to restricted confidence is coherent and avoids inferring that nothing at all can be known.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The missing non-Christian evidence is specifically identified, but the move does not analyze why the surviving sources cannot independently reach narrower conclusions.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move expressly connects evidential underdetermination to withholding the bodily-resurrection conclusion, directly supporting the con motion bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: Flew expressly acknowledges that there is evidence for a list of claims while distinguishing that from confident knowledge of what happened.

moves.evidenceBasis: Flew cites the enormous shortage of non-Christian evidence, acknowledges an evidential fact list, and places it against a background of extensive historical ignorance.

moves.speaker: Antony Flew
moves.proposition: The Thomas narrative reports sight and an invitation to touch but does not clearly report that Thomas actually touched Jesus, so it does not establish physical contact with a risen body.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator asks Flew whether he accepts the four facts, and Flew personally develops the Thomas-based qualification to literal appearances.

components.text: Whether the reported appearances include adequately evidenced physical contact with a risen body.
Whether early Pauline testimony independently reports Thomas touching Jesus.
Whether the Thomas narrative defeats a nonphysical interpretation of appearance experiences.

response.rationale: The reply directly qualifies one prominent physical-contact narrative by distinguishing an invitation to touch from a report that touching occurred.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts a decisive physicality example but only partially answers the broader appearance case, which includes other texts and observations.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction between an invitation and an actual reported touch is precise, explicitly confined to the Thomas narrative.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Flew uses qualified language about what he can see in the narrative and does not claim that the passage disproves bodily resurrection.

charity.alternative: The invitation, visual encounter, and Thomas's response may still imply a physical body without an explicit touch report.
charity.decisiveQualification: Such implication is weaker than direct textual testimony that Thomas actually made physical contact.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference is valid and narrow: absence of a reported completed touch prevents this passage alone from establishing actual contact.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The argument closely tracks the narrative distinction, though the excerpt does not quote the complete passage or address its broader context.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It is highly relevant within the subsidiary physical-texts tier but does not by itself reach the full central nonbodily burden.

representationalCharity.rationale: The objection fairly targets the limited textual claim and does not deny that the narrative contains an invitation or other appearance evidence.

moves.evidenceBasis: Flew notes Thomas's doubts, the invitation to put his hands into the wounds, and the absence of an explicit statement that Thomas actually did so.

moves.speaker: Gary Habermas
moves.proposition: Johannine and Gospel testimony to touching, close observation, eating, and Jesus' denial that he was a spirit supports the claim that witnesses reported a literal physical resurrection body.
moves.attributionBasis: Habermas responds in the first person with a connected citation-based argument from First John and Luke about seeing and touching Jesus.

components.text: Whether the textual record contains physical-contact evidence beyond an uncompleted invitation to Thomas.
Whether the reports include concrete publicly observable bodily characteristics.
Whether touching, eating, and denial of being a spirit exclude vision-only interpretations.
Whether these Gospel and Johannine sources are independent and historically reliable.

response.rationale: Habermas answers the narrow Thomas objection with other touching, eating, and anti-spirit texts, while leaving the earlier source-independence challenge unresolved.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The reply fully contacts the physical-text component but remains a partial answer to the broader historical-warrant and corroboration challenge.

precisionFindings.rationale: The physicality claim and textual indicators are clear, with an implicit qualification that these establish what was reported rather than what occurred.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Multiple physical indicators support the report-content claim, but saying the evidence shows a literal body compresses source reliability and narrative dependence.

charity.alternative: Thomas may not have touched Jesus, and physical narrative details may be later literary development.
charity.decisiveQualification: Other texts report touching, eating, and explicit denial of spirit status, although their historical reliability remains separately contestable.

logicalCoherence.rationale: If the cited reports are historically reliable, touching, eating, and denial of spirit status strongly support a bodily interpretation; that conditional is implicit.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move provides several specific textual features but does not establish their dating, independence, eyewitness status, or historical reliability.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central bodily-appearances bridge through multiple claimed physical interactions and observations.

representationalCharity.rationale: Habermas answers the strongest narrow textual objection with independent physical details but does not address the live source-development qualification.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt cites hands touching, Jesus's invitation to touch, his denial that he was a ghost, eating, and repeated seeing and touching by the witnesses.

moves.speaker: Gary Habermas
moves.proposition: Paul's terminology and stated beliefs in First Corinthians 15 and Philippians 3 indicate bodily transformation and physical resurrection rather than a disembodied spirit.
moves.attributionBasis: After the break Habermas resumes his explicitly identified argument about Paul's understanding, continuing through the delivered boundary context.

components.text: Whether Paul's own language supplies a sufficiently specific bodily interpretation of resurrection.
Whether physical resurrection depends solely on the Thomas touch narrative.
Whether Paul's experience should be interpreted only as a disembodied conversion phenomenon.
Whether Pauline testimony has adequate external corroboration.

response.rationale: The move uses Pauline terminology to answer nonphysical interpretations of Paul and reduces dependence on Thomas, but does not repair the external-corroboration gap.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive conceptual issue in Paul's evidence while leaving source independence and the phenomenology of Damascus only partly addressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The bodily-transformation claim is clear, but the spoken contrast among spirit, spiritual, and body is linguistically compressed and partly unstable.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The cited terminology supports bodily transformation, though the conclusion that it specifies a physical Damascus encounter requires additional exegesis.

charity.alternative: A spiritual body may denote transformed embodiment without implying ordinary material characteristics or a tactile Damascus encounter.
charity.decisiveQualification: Transformed embodiment is still bodily language, but it does not alone determine every physical property or appearance mode.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from bodily-transformation vocabulary to some embodied resurrection is plausible, but a material bridge to ordinary physicality remains unstated.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Specific Pauline passages and lexical contrasts are identified, while the underlying Greek, context, and rival readings are not sufficiently defended.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly bears on the central bodily-appearances bridge by interpreting the earliest named witness's resurrection concept.

representationalCharity.rationale: Habermas recognizes the adjective spiritual but moves too quickly from substantive body language to a fully physical interpretation of the encounter.

moves.evidenceBasis: Habermas contrasts spirit terminology with Paul's use of body in First Corinthians 15 and invokes three statements in Philippians 3 as bodily-transformation evidence.

moves.speaker: Antony Flew
moves.proposition: Describing a body as spiritual or immaterial does not identify bodily characteristics and therefore does not by itself provide a coherent account of a genuinely physical resurrection body.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator directly invites Flew to answer, and the ensuing first-person response is continuous until the next question.

components.text: Whether the expression spiritual body coherently establishes the characteristics required for a physical resurrection body.
Whether the Gospel touching and eating reports independently specify physical characteristics.
Whether reported appearances establish an identifiable bodily entity.

response.rationale: Flew directly challenges the conceptual inference from spiritual body to physical body, but does not engage the separate touching, eating, and observation texts.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The decisive Pauline terminology component is contacted, while the broader physical-encounter case remains unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The conceptual objection is recoverable, but spiritual and immaterial are treated as near equivalents without an explicit defense of that equivalence.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The categorical claim that an immaterial substance is nothing and a spiritual body no body exceeds the conceptual argument actually supplied.

charity.alternative: Spiritual may characterize a transformed body's governing mode rather than deny all embodiment or material continuity.
charity.decisiveQualification: The phrase still requires a positive account of bodily characteristics before it independently establishes physicality.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The demand for specified characteristics is legitimate, but equating spiritual, immaterial, and nonexistent introduces substantial equivocation.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move is largely a conceptual assertion and provides no textual or philosophical defense for its decisive equivalences.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central bodily-appearances bridge through the meaning of Pauline resurrection language, though with limited reach beyond that text.

representationalCharity.rationale: Flew identifies the need for positive characteristics but materially weakens the alternative by equating spiritual with immaterial and then with nothing.

moves.evidenceBasis: Flew argues that calling a body spiritual supplies no recognizable characteristic, equates the term with immateriality, and concludes it is not genuinely a body.

moves.speaker: Antony Flew
moves.proposition: What it is rational to conclude from an alleged miracle depends on prior beliefs, so the same report may rationally support resurrection for a believer while leaving a skeptic rationally suspecting error.
moves.attributionBasis: Habermas asks Flew directly what he thinks, and Flew answers in the first person while contrasting his outlook with Jewish and Christian priors.

components.text: Whether evidence interpreted as bodily resurrection can rationally establish a miracle independently of prior beliefs.
Whether extraordinary physical-encounter reports overcome a skeptic's prior expectation of error.
Whether the historical fact list alone determines the resurrection conclusion.

response.rationale: The reply directly reframes the evidential dispute in terms of prior probability and explains why the same alleged miracle report can rationally be assessed differently.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts the inference from extraordinary reports to miracle, though it does not quantify or independently justify either party's priors.

precisionFindings.rationale: The conditional dependence of rational judgment on prior belief is clear and confined to alleged miracles and apparently extraordinary reports.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Flew states what is rational from his stated prior position without claiming that error has been demonstrated with certainty.

charity.alternative: A believer with justified theistic priors may rationally treat the same evidence as supporting resurrection.
charity.decisiveQualification: Different conclusions are rational only insofar as the competing prior beliefs themselves are justified and updated consistently.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The dependence of posterior judgment on priors is coherent, with the important but bounded implicit premise that the priors are themselves rationally held.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The general probabilistic point is well supported conceptually, but no comparative evidence is supplied for the actual strength of the relevant priors.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central miracle-background bridge by making antecedent commitments indispensable to the miracle inference.

representationalCharity.rationale: Flew expressly grants that rational assessment can differ for someone with different priors, while preserving the need to evaluate those priors.

moves.evidenceBasis: Flew explicitly states that rational assessment of an alleged miracle depends on prior belief and contrasts a believer's possible conclusion with his own suspicion of mistake.

moves.speaker: Gary Habermas
moves.proposition: Jesus' death by crucifixion is supported by medical considerations, critical consensus, non-Christian sources, Pauline testimony, and the failure of survival scenarios.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator asks Habermas for sources, and the response identifies scholarly, medical, extra-biblical, and Pauline grounds in an extended answer.

components.text: Whether the sparse record nonetheless supports the narrower conclusion that Jesus actually died by crucifixion.
Whether non-Christian and multidisciplinary evidence corroborates the death claim.
Whether survival rather than postmortem experience remains a viable explanation.
Whether establishing death independently establishes the later miracle conclusion.

response.rationale: Habermas answers general historical skepticism on the narrower death premise through several evidence types and attacks survival scenarios, without resolving the miracle inference.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It gives a strong partial answer concerning death and corroboration but does not answer underdetermination of the later resurrection event.

precisionFindings.rationale: The death-by-crucifixion proposition and its evidence classes are clear, with an implicit distinction between consensus and direct evidence.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The convergent evidence warrants very high confidence in death, but quoted language that it is as sure as anything is somewhat stronger than the span's documentation.

charity.alternative: Sparse ancient evidence may leave room for survival or uncertainty about the precise manner of death.
charity.decisiveQualification: Multiple independent evidence types can establish death strongly even if they do not establish resurrection.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The convergence of medical, critical, non-Christian, and Pauline considerations coherently supports actual death and constrains survival explanations.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Several specific evidence classes and named skeptical scholars are supplied, with a bounded gap in presenting the medical and extra-biblical details.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move is exceptionally relevant within the subsidiary death-and-tomb tier but does not independently complete a central or motion bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: Habermas directly addresses survival and sparse-source concerns with convergent evidence while keeping the death premise distinct from the whole resurrection case.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt invokes medical data, scholarly criticism, extra-biblical sources, Pauline testimony, named Jesus Seminar scholars, and the inadequacyacy of survival scenarios.

moves.speaker: Gary Habermas
moves.proposition: The empty tomb is supported by early accounts, hostile acknowledgment, proclamation in Jerusalem, and the counterproductive identification of women as its primary witnesses.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator requests the grounds for an empty tomb, and Habermas gives a numbered, continuous set of historical considerations before inviting Flew's response.

components.text: Whether the available ancient record supplies cumulative grounds for accepting an empty burial place.
Whether multiple and hostile sources provide meaningful corroboration of the empty tomb.
Whether an empty tomb independently establishes bodily contact or appearance.
Whether the empty tomb alone warrants a miracle conclusion.

response.rationale: The move supplies several cumulative considerations for the empty tomb and addresses corroboration, while appropriately leaving bodily appearance and miracle identification to other moves.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive tomb-evidence component but only partially answers the broader historical and miracle underdetermination challenges.

precisionFindings.rationale: The cumulative case is clear, but hostile acknowledgment and the number and independence of sources are somewhat broadly characterized.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The considerations support an empty-tomb inference, though hostile admission and source multiplicity require qualifications not expressed in the excerpt.

charity.alternative: The empty-tomb traditions may share dependence, and hostile explanations need not independently verify every narrative detail.
charity.decisiveQualification: Even dependent or hostile traditions can add some cumulative support, but their evidential weight depends on dating and independence.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The several considerations can coherently accumulate toward an empty tomb, although no one item uniquely entails the conclusion.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Specific textual, hostile-attestation, Jerusalem-proclamation, and women-witness considerations are offered, but independence and transmission warrants are compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly and strongly supports the subsidiary death-and-tomb bridge while stopping short of the bodily-resurrection conclusion.

representationalCharity.rationale: Habermas offers a genuine cumulative case but does not engage the strongest dependence and dating qualifications affecting its sources.

moves.evidenceBasis: Habermas invokes early creedal sequences, alleged Jewish acknowledgment in three sources, Jerusalem proclamation, and women as counterproductive invented witnesses.

moves.speaker: Antony Flew
moves.proposition: Even if the tomb was empty, the absence of independent witnesses leaves many possible ways the body could have been removed, and the available ancient evidence cannot satisfactorily reconstruct what occurred.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator asks Flew what happened to the body, and Flew answers in the first person while expressly declining to offer a definite reconstruction.

components.text: Whether an accepted empty tomb uniquely or confidently identifies what happened to Jesus's body.
Whether actual death excludes later removal of the body.
Whether appearance reports independently eliminate unknown removal scenarios.
Whether the historical core permits a complete reconstruction of the burial aftermath.

response.rationale: Flew grants the issue conditionally and directly argues that an empty tomb underdetermines removal, while declining to invent one unsupported detailed scenario.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive uniqueness inference from the empty tomb but does not compare removal possibilities against the appearance evidence.

precisionFindings.rationale: The proposition is carefully limited to epistemic underdetermination and expressly avoids claiming a specific reconstructed removal story.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Flew claims only that multiple removal possibilities remain and that the record cannot reconstruct one confidently, matching the evidence offered.

charity.alternative: The empty tomb combined with appearances and hostile acknowledgment may disfavor ordinary removal scenarios.
charity.decisiveQualification: Such cumulative evidence may reduce removal probability, but an empty tomb alone does not identify the remover or cause.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from an unwitnessed empty tomb to multiple unresolved removal possibilities is valid and does not require selecting one speculative theory.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Absence of independent witnesses supports uncertainty, but the move does not provide concrete historical removal evidence or comparative likelihoods.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central alternative-underdetermination bridge by showing that the tomb condition does not uniquely select resurrection.

representationalCharity.rationale: Flew confines his conclusion to underdetermination rather than asserting theft, though he does not fully compare removal with the appearance evidence.

moves.evidenceBasis: Flew emphasizes the lack of independent witnesses, the many possible ways bodies may be removed, and his inability to reconstruct a detailed ancient-city narrative.

moves.speaker: Gary Habermas
moves.proposition: Combining distinct hallucination accounts for Paul and the disciples with an unexplained removal of the body compounds unsupported assumptions rather than producing a coherent explanation of the combined evidence.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly turns to Habermas and asks him to survey naturalistic alternatives, which he does through a sustained first-person analysis.

components.text: Whether combining unknown body removal with distinct psychological accounts yields an adequate explanation of all asserted evidence.
Whether separate accounts for Paul and the disciples jointly explain the appearance reports.
Whether historical ignorance itself supplies a positive rival explanation.
Whether the asserted evidence set is independently reliable.
Whether Pauline spiritual-body language coherently establishes physicality.
Whether resurrection has adequate antecedent probability.

response.rationale: Habermas directly challenges the cumulative scope and conjunctive cost of the proposed alternatives, but assumes the evidence set and does not answer source, conceptual, or prior objections.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The reply contacts the decisive comparative-scope component while remaining partial across several independent challenges to its premises and priors.

precisionFindings.rationale: The conjunction-cost argument is clear, though the exact set of alternatives and what counts as an unsupported assumption remain partly unspecified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move correctly notes cumulative explanatory costs, but saying the alternatives do not work exceeds the comparative evidence developed in this excerpt.

charity.alternative: Different causes may explain different facts, and an underdetermination case need not offer one unified naturalistic theory.
charity.decisiveQualification: Plural causes remain possible, but their conjunction must still be assessed for independent support and total explanatory scope.

moves.speaker: Antony Flew
moves.proposition: Identifying an extraordinary event as a miracle requires justified prior beliefs about a supernatural power and supplementary beliefs about that power's nature and intentions, not merely an unusual report.
moves.attributionBasis: Habermas hands the discussion to Flew by name, and the response articulates Flew's qualified agreement and required theological background conditions.

response.rationale: Flew directly sharpens the prior challenge by requiring justified belief in supernatural power plus beliefs about its nature and intentions before labeling an event a miracle.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The reply explicitly contacts the decisive missing warrant in the proposed theistic background and states its consequence for miracle identification.

precisionFindings.rationale: The necessary background conditions are clearly distinguished from the unusual report and confined to identifying an event as a miracle.
